newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finland ties knot with Europe through currency link.
newsitem.headline: Finland ties knot with Europe through currency link.

text.p: New European Union member Finland took another decisive step westward over the weekend, leapfrogging over powerful neighbour Sweden to link its currency to Europe's stability mechanism and possibly qualify for a single currency in 1999.

With Saturday's agreement to join the EU currency grid, Finland has proclaimed its determination to be in the first wave of countries to join Europe's planned Economic and Monetary Union at its start in 1999.
The ERM, which limits currency fluctuations to at most 15 percent up or down, now groups 11 of the EU's 15 currencies. Sweden, Britain, Italy and Greece remain outside.

Helsinki's decision was "not a surprise and confirms the positive political sentiment in favour of European monetary union throughout Europe," said Gerrard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.

The move was widely anticipated by financial markets and welcomed in Bonn and Paris, but came amid domestic fears for the competitiveness of Finland's export industries, and a union source said it would spell trouble for the coalition government.

The European Union's monetary committee decided Saturday to bring the markka, floating for the past four years, into its Exchange Rate Mechanism currency grid at a central rate of 3.04 to the German mark.

Finland joined the EU with Sweden in 1995, after decades of treading an East-West tightrope in the shadow of the Soviet Union. Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen has said he sees security in binding the non-aligned country as tightly as possible to Brussels.
"The reasons are perhaps more to do with security policy than economic issues," Atte Jaaskelainen of leading daily Helsingin Sanomat wrote in a commentary Sunday.
Political commentators also celebrated the fact that Finland -- which was part of Sweden until 1809 and has tended to follow its larger western neighbour -- was able to move first.

"By separating itself from its neighbour's pace, Finland has lifted itself spiritually closer to the European core for which Sweden, by its size, resources and traditions, is better equipped than Finland," wrote daily Turun Sanomat.

But many have warned the link -- at a relatively strong level for the markka against Sweden's crown -- could also hurt Finland's key pulp and paper exporters, by closing the door to competitive devaluations while Sweden still retains that option.
In Stockholm, the Swedish central bank said Finland's ERM membership would not affect Sweden's position that it did not have to join the grid to qualify for the new single currency.

Official reactions from Finnish industry were muted, but one key labour union official angrily said the link would only have been tolerable at a much weaker 3.15 to the German mark and promised trouble at the next round of central contract talks in 1997.

Finland's coalition government -- which has been rewarded for fiscal austerity by financial markets -- has earned credibility also through Lipponen's connections with unions, which helped foster a two-year wage stability pact last year.
The Bank of Finland said Saturday that future exchange rate stability meant wage developments must continue on a moderate course. The union source said this was now at risk.

"Branch by branch, industrial unions, particularly in the export sector, will go out and take all that they can get. This means we're kissing goodbye to the chances of a centralized pay deal," the source warned.

Coming just one week before local and municipal elections, the move was also seen by commentators as a show of force -- and possibly a handy distraction from the tough question of joblessness -- for Lipponen, whose five-party coalition holds 142 of parliament's 200 seats.
"It's one possibility to catch media attention and make sure there will be no room for discussion (of the jobless issue)," said Sammy Borg, political scientist at Tampere University.

Finnish unemployment, about 16 percent in August, is at one of Europe's highest levels, and the government has shown little solid progress in a pledge to bring it to around 8 percent or 9 percent by the end of its term in 1999.
